concept.name: Nominal GDP
concept.definition: Gross domestic product measured at the market prices prevailing during the period being measured, without adjustment for inflation. It moves with both the quantity of output and the price level.
concept.intuition: Nominal GDP is the raw dollar size of the economy; it grows even if the country produces the same amount, simply because everything costs more.
concept.mechanics: BEA values current-period final output at current-period prices (current-dollar estimates). Comparing nominal GDP across periods mixes volume and price changes, so analysts deflate it to obtain real GDP.
concept.formula: Nominal GDP = sum over goods i of (P_i,t x Q_i,t), where P_i,t and Q_i,t are current-period prices and quantities of final goods and services.
concept.failure_modes: In high-inflation episodes nominal GDP can look strong while real output stagnates; cross-period or cross-country comparisons in nominal terms conflate price-level differences with size differences.
concept.misconceptions: Nominal GDP is not 'wrong' or useless — it is the right denominator for debt-to-GDP and tax-revenue ratios, since debts and revenues are nominal; it is only misleading when used to infer real growth.
concept.example: U.S. nominal GDP grew briskly in 2021-2022, but a large share of that increase was price inflation, which is why real GDP grew much more slowly over the same period.

citations.source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis — Gross Domestic Product (Learning Center)
